title: State v. Tobin Hale
summary: Marek Lindqvist, night supervisor at Harbor Cold Storage, was found dead in a chilled corridor at 6 AM, killed by a blow to the head. Tobin Hale, 34, a forklift operator from Dockside Estate, was fired by Lindqvist that afternoon. Hale says he came back that night for his tools and left by 11:40 PM.

evidence.label: The badge log
evidence.detail: Hale's badge opened the dock door at 11:52 PM. An IT audit found the reader's clock can drift up to 9 minutes, and staff admit they shared badges.

evidence.label: The pry bar
evidence.detail: Found near the body with the victim's blood and a 9-point partial print matching Hale. Hale used this bar on most shifts.

evidence.label: The text message
evidence.detail: At 5:10 PM Hale texted a coworker: "He'll pay for this." Hale had booked an employment lawyer for the next morning.

evidence.label: The dock video
evidence.detail: A hooded figure crosses the dock at 11:58 PM, roughly Hale's height. The camera records 2 frames a second and shows no face.

evidence.label: Time of death
evidence.detail: Estimated at 11:30 PM to 12:30 AM. The medical examiner agreed the cold corridor could widen that by 45 minutes either way.

evidence.label: The phone ping
evidence.detail: Hale's phone used a tower near the dock at 12:14 AM. The same tower also covers his flat.

evidence.label: The second glove
evidence.detail: A bloodstained work glove was found by the dock door. It was never tested.

evidence.label: The prior conviction
evidence.detail: Hale has one assault conviction, from when he was 19. There has been nothing in the 15 years since.

witnesses.name: Inez Porter
witnesses.statement: Heard shouting around midnight and says she knew Tobin's voice. She was behind a freezer door next to the compressors. She had reported Hale twice before.

witnesses.name: Priya Nand
witnesses.statement: Received the text. Says Hale was "all talk" and that he was crying when he told her he'd been fired.

witnesses.name: Det. Sol Brandt
witnesses.statement: Named Hale as the suspect within an hour of arriving. Admitted under cross-examination that the glove was never sent to the lab.

witnesses.name: Owen Lund
witnesses.statement: Says Lindqvist had been skimming stock and owed money to someone on the day shift.

points.claim: His badge opened the door after he says he left
The victim's blood and his print are on the weapon
He threatened the victim hours before
The figure on video matches his height
He'd been fired by the victim that same day
Even with clock drift, 11:43 still doesn't match his 11:40
His phone was near the dock after midnight
He has been violent before
The badge clock drifts up to 9 minutes
Staff shared badges, so a badge isn't a person
He used that bar daily, so his print proves nothing
He'd booked a lawyer, so 'pay' may mean a lawsuit
2 frames a second and no face identifies nobody
The cold widens time of death by 45 minutes each way
That tower also covers his flat
Nobody can identify a voice through a freezer door beside compressors
Porter had reported him twice, so she expected it to be him
A bloodstained glove was never tested
The detective picked his suspect within an hour
The victim's skimming gave someone else a motive
15 clean years mean the conviction says little
He was crying, not plotting, when he told Priya

record.reason: The state put Hale near the scene and gave him a reason to be angry. It never placed him at the body. The print is explained by his job, the voice was heard through a freezer door, and the one object that could have settled it, a bloodstained glove, was never sent to the lab. That is reasonable doubt.

beats: Tobin Hale did come back for his tools. He left by 11:40, as he said.
He got as far as his van, and he sat there. Then he went back in.
His badge opened the dock door at 11:52. The clock was right that night, and nobody had borrowed it.
He only wanted Marek Lindqvist to say it to his face. Lindqvist laughed at him in the cold corridor. The pry bar was where it always was.
One blow. Inez Porter knew his voice after all.
He sat in the van until 12:14, not able to turn the key. Then he drove home.

Every fact in his favour was true. He had booked the lawyer. He meant the lawsuit when he sent that text. He cried when he told Priya. Lindqvist really was skimming, and it had nothing to do with anything.
The second glove was his. One lab test would have ended the argument in that room. It was never sent.
truth.closing: Twelve strangers are only ever given what the state can show. That is the promise of reasonable doubt, and this is what it costs.
